title: Wide-field mid- to long-wave infrared imaging with undetected photons
authors: Vladimir Kornienko, Nathan Gemmell, Caiyi Liu, Asteria Chen, Chris Phillips, Rupert Oulton
abstract: Quantum imaging with undetected photons (QIUP) allows an object to be probed at mid-infrared frequencies by only measuring interference in the visible range, thus leveraging silicon camera technology. We show that non-collinear phase-matching in a silver thiogallate (AgGaS$_2$) crystal enables wide-field QIUP in the wavelength range of 6-10 $μ$m (1670-1000 cm$^{-1}$). A combination of coherent detection and infrared photons being ``undetected'' enables imaging at ${\sim}$100 times better than the background-limited infrared photodetection (BLIP) limit. At 8 $μ$m, our images have over 8000 $\pm$ 100 resolvable elements with a 297 $\pm$ 5 $μ$m resolution, and 10 s acquisition time. Our results pave the way to fast, background-noise-free, room-temperature, spectrally-selective mid-infrared imaging.
summary: This paper reports on a quantum imaging technique using undetected photons (QIUP) to achieve mid- to long-wave infrared imaging. By measuring visible light interference patterns modulated by mid-IR light passing through an object, the method bypasses background noise limitations. This enables fast, room-temperature, and spectrally-selective imaging in the 6-10 $\mu$m range.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of performing wide-field mid- to long-wave infrared (IR) imaging by overcoming the limitations imposed by background-limited infrared photodetection (BLIP).
main_result: They successfully demonstrated wide-field quantum imaging with undetected photons (QIUP) in the 6-10 $\mu$m range, achieving background-noise-free imaging with high resolution.
method: The technique uses nonlinear interferometry where the object modifies the interference pattern of a visible 'signal' beam, while the mid-IR 'idler' beam passes through the object undetected.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes non-collinear phase-matching in a silver thiogallate (AgGaS2) crystal, generating signal and idler photons via SPDC. The measurement relies on extracting object transmittance from the interference visibility.
key_observables: Image resolution ($297 \pm 5 \ \mu	ext{m}$ at $8 \ \mu	ext{m}$), number of resolvable elements ($\sim 8000$), and interference pattern visibility ($V$).
important_parameters: Wavelength range of 6-10 $\mu$m; background-limited infrared photodetection (BLIP) limit; 10 s acquisition time.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes the idler beam passes the object twice, and that a large difference in beam diameters is used to separate signal and idler beams.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the nonlinear interferometry setup, raw camera images showing interference, and resolution estimation using a knife-edge test.
paper_structure: The paper details the QIUP principle, describes the experimental setup using SPDC and $	ext{AgGaS}_2$, presents measurements of visibility and resolution, and concludes with the demonstration of fast, background-noise-free mid-IR imaging.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it demonstrates a novel, background-noise-free quantum measurement technique for probing inaccessible spectral regions (mid-IR).

Bringing the knife edge close to the optical axis of the system results in the blade shadow appearing in both signal and idler beams. Three regions in the image can be observed: R1 – signal beam is blocked, intensity is halved, no interference observed; R2 – all three beams are intact, nonlinear interference is observed; R3 – blocking the idler in R1 leads to distinguishability in the photon pairs, thus no interference is observed in the signal beam, but the signal beam intensity is unaffected.
